 Saving Morale During Daylight Saving
 Anjeza Gashi , Contributing Writer 
 Nov 11, 2026 
 Courtesy of City of Arlington Daylight Saving Time means shorter days and darker nights, but there are many ways to keep your spirits up. 
 Nov. 1 has come and gone, which means we have once again lost an hour of our day due to the clocks being set back. Although we may appreciate the extra hour of sleep, the earlier sunsets can be disappointing. After a long and tiring semester filled with classes, assignments, work and extracurricular activities, the earlier sunsets can feel like a weight has been placed on your shoulders. However, there are some things you can do to keep your spirits up. 
 During this time of long, cold nights, many people suffer from seasonal affective disorder (SAD). This is a type of depression that can temporarily make you feel tired, experience changes in sleep patterns and struggle to concentrate. However, not everyone who feels the winter blues suffers from SAD, and it’s important to recognize that there are ways to get past these low feelings. 
 First, get some sunshine. Take a short walk outside during your breaks. It may be chilly outside, but take a quick walk, get a coffee, call a friend or just sit outside for a few minutes. If you’re unable to walk outside at lunchtime, try to sit by a window while you’re studying. It may not fix everything, but getting outside can be a nice way to refresh. 
 Try exercising; you don’t have to spend an intense hour at the gym. You could attend a fitness class on campus, play outdoor games with friends or even just do some stretches in your room. Doing a short workout will help get your mind off things, improve your energy levels and lift your mood. As the days get shorter and colder, we often feel like staying in our warm beds all day, however, getting your body moving will help you feel more awake. Do something that you actually enjoy so you can look forward to doing it again. 
 Find a new hobby. With the arrival of shorter days, it is the perfect opportunity to find something new and interesting or to continue doing the things that bring joy. Knitting, crocheting, painting, journaling, baking, playing an instrument — all of these are hobbies that can help take your mind off the stress of studying and give you an exciting activity to do. You do not need to be good at them, you just need to unwind, let the creativity flow and enjoy the leisure time. Who knows, maybe it will become your passion! 
 It is important to try to keep the same routine. If you are staying up late and going to classes early in the morning, you will feel exhausted. Try maintaining your sleeping schedule, eating healthy food regularly and taking breaks from using your phone or scrolling social media feeds. Create a mini-routine every evening, like making yourself a cup of tea, reading a chapter of a book or listening to some music. 
 Always plan something. While it may be tempting to forget making plans because it is dark and cold outside, socializing with people can help you deal with the loneliness of this challenging period. Have dinner with friends, attend some events on campus or simply watch a film. You do not need to spend any money or effort, and having something to look forward to will make the whole week better. 
 Do not forget about relaxation. While feeling guilty about a lack of motivation when you have a lot of work is natural, you need to split the assignments or tasks into parts and congratulate yourself on completing them. No matter whether you have spent 20 minutes studying, cleaning your room or going to sleep earlier than usual, you have done something good for yourself. 
 Despite the earlier sunset, sometimes it is enough to simply step out and enjoy the daylight.
